brief.headline: The UK and EU have agreed a food trade deal that would cut SPS paperwork and border checks, while the UK carbon border charge starts on 1 January 2027 and will apply to Moroccan fertiliser imports unless emissions are declared.
brief.overview: The UK and EU struck a food and plants trade deal at the EU-UK Summit, though no start date has been given and existing SPS rules still apply until it takes effect. From 1 January 2027 the UK carbon border adjustment mechanism will add a carbon cost to fertiliser imports from Morocco unless importers declare verified actual emissions. In Morocco, exporters may gain duty-free access to China under a new measure, subject to rules of origin and ADII certificates. Across the wider network, Hormuz traffic remains about 65% below pre-conflict levels, Los Angeles and Long Beach face a possible labour disruption that a tentative deal has eased, and Spain has announced a national scrubber washwater ban from July 2027.

highlights.text: The UK carbon border charge applies to Moroccan fertiliser imports from 1 January 2027 unless importers declare verified actual emissions.
Moroccan exports to China may be exempt from Chinese customs duties, but proof of origin meeting Chinese rules will be needed.
The UK and EU food trade deal could cut certificates, documentation and border checks once it takes effect, with no start date yet.
Spain will ban scrubber wastewater discharge in all its ports and anchorages from 1 July 2027.
A tentative agreement covering about 250 watchmen at Los Angeles and Long Beach lowers the immediate strike risk, pending ratification.
Hormuz transits stayed about 65% below pre-conflict levels, with six tankers attacked in the week.

deadlines.text: Los Angeles and Long Beach port contract expires at 12:01 on Saturday, a possible watchmen strike date.
Contract extension expires for LA-Long Beach port security workers, the strike deadline cited by trade groups.
IMO Marine Environment Protection Committee meets to consider the Net-Zero Framework.
Hapag-Lloyd Equipment Imbalance Surcharge applies to intra-Asia shipments to Vietnam for dry and refrigerated containers.
Maersk Intermodal Fuel Fee for UK full-container landside moves rises to 11.6% for truck or rail, and Ireland's truck fee is 8.1%.
UK carbon border adjustment mechanism starts, covering aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen, iron and steel.
Hapag-Lloyd Marine Fuel Surcharge applies to all new contracts, gradually replacing the Marine Fuel Recovery mechanism.
Spain's ban on scrubber wastewater discharge in its ports and anchorages takes effect for all scrubber types.

brief.market: Asia to US container rates were mostly lower, with Drewry reporting falls of 5% to Los Angeles and 9% to New York, while US Gulf chemical tanker rates were mostly higher. Reduced Hormuz transit capacity raises the risk of delays and cost pressure on Gulf-linked energy and LPG cargo. Maersk's higher UK fuel fee and Hapag-Lloyd's Vietnam imbalance surcharge will add to landside and intra-Asia costs from December 2026.

items.title: Hormuz traffic stays 65% below pre-war levels as six tankers attacked
items.originalTitle: Strait Of Hormuz Traffic Stays 65% Below Pre-War Levels As 6 Tankers Are Attacked In A Week
items.summary: Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz stayed about 65% below pre-conflict levels in mid-November, with 263 transits in the seven days to 18 November, down from 308 the week before. UKMTO reported attacks on six tankers in the week, including two in the Persian Gulf, and one crew member was reported missing on each of two affected vessels. The JMIC rates the threat level in the strait as severe.
items.impact: Reduced transit capacity through the strait raises the risk of delays and cost pressure on Gulf-linked cargo, particularly energy and LPG. Attacks near Khasab and the strait itself make war-risk cover, crew safety and routing decisions central to planning. UKMTO cannot verify all US-facilitated transits, so official counts may understate the true incident picture.
items.action: Check with carriers and war-risk insurers on routing, surcharges and sailing reliability for Gulf calls, and watch UKMTO and JMIC updates before committing to Hormuz transits.
keyFigures: 263 vessel transits in the seven days to 18 November, down from 308
Six tankers attacked in one week, with four in the strait and two in the Persian Gulf
106 incidents recorded in the strait since 28 February 2026
About 10% of attacked vessels with confirmed outcomes lost or sunk since 17 August

items.title: Possible LA/LB port strike this weekend as Asia-US container rates ease
items.originalTitle: Asia-US container rates lower, tanker rates ex-USG higher; possible strike at LA/LB ports this weekend
items.summary: Talks between ILWU Local 26 and the Pacific Maritime Association ended without agreement, raising the possibility of a watchmen strike at the Los Angeles and Long Beach port complex after the contract expires at 12:01 on Saturday 21 November. Container rates from Asia to the US were mostly lower, with Drewry reporting falls of 5% to Los Angeles and 9% to New York, while US Gulf chemical tanker rates were mostly higher on the USG-to-ARA and USG-to-Brazil lanes.
items.impact: A strike could halt operations at eight terminals and affect vessel, yard and gate activity, with a significant rail backlog already slowing inland moves of holiday inventory. Analysts expect limited effect on Black Friday goods, but other holiday cargo still in port could face delays and some deliveries may be threatened.
items.action: Importers and forwarders shipping into LA/LB should check cargo status, prepare contingency routings and monitor the contract outcome after the Saturday expiry.
keyFigures: Rates to West Coast $7,025-8,460/FEU
Rates to East Coast $8,194-10,900/FEU
Drewry Shanghai-Los Angeles down 5%, Shanghai-New York down 9%
ILWU Local 26 covers about 250 port watchmen handling roughly 85% of Long Beach cargo

items.title: UK carbon border charge hits Moroccan fertiliser imports from January 2027
items.originalTitle: Le Royaume-Uni soumet les engrais marocains à une vérification carbone propre à son mécanisme frontal
items.summary: HMRC has set out how UK importers can declare the actual emissions of goods under the UK carbon border adjustment mechanism, which starts on 1 January 2027 and covers aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen, iron and steel. Importers can use verified actual emissions or HMRC default values, and the verifier must hold a process-specific accreditation to ISO/IEC 17029 and ISO 14065. The charge applies the sectoral quarterly rate to embedded emissions, less any carbon price already paid in the country of production.
items.impact: Moroccan fertiliser exports to the UK will carry a carbon cost from 2027, unless the importer declares actual emissions verified by an accredited third party. Default values are binding once chosen and cannot be corrected later, and they are set high for ammonia and nitric acid, so the default route may be costly for some producers. Registration is needed for importers buying at least £50,000 of covered goods in a 30-day window or having passed that amount in the previous twelve months, with the first declaration and payment due by 31 May 2028.
items.action: Moroccan producers and their UK clients should decide now whether to use actual or default emissions, and start monitoring emissions over the full calendar year 2027 with an accredited verifier. Producers should prepare to pass CN code, net weight, verified emissions intensity, intermediate material data and any carbon taxes paid in Morocco to UK customers.
keyFigures: Default value for anhydrous ammonia: 2.4 t CO2e per tonne
Registration threshold: £50,000 of covered goods
Materiality threshold: 5% of emissions intensity
First declaration and payment due by 31 May 2028

items.title: China grants duty-free access to Moroccan exports under new African measure
items.originalTitle: La Chine ouvre son marché au Maroc: les exportations exemptées de droits de douane
items.summary: Moroccan exports to China are now exempt from customs duties under a new Chinese trade measure for African countries, according to Morocco's Ministry of Foreign Trade. Access to the preferential treatment depends on compliance with the rules of origin notified by China and annexed to the ministry's notice. ADII remains responsible for issuing the certificates of origin required for export, and other export formalities are unchanged.
items.impact: Moroccan exporters could sell to China without paying Chinese import duties, which may improve margins and competitiveness on eligible products. Forwarders and exporters will need proof of origin that meets the Chinese rules, so documentation through ADII will be central to claiming the benefit. The article gives no effective date, product list or start date for the measure, so the scope remains unclear.
items.action: Exporters and forwarders should obtain the Chinese rules of origin annexed to the ministry notice and check which HS codes are covered. Confirm the certificate of origin procedure with ADII before shipping, and watch for the effective date and product scope.
keyFigures: Trade between China and Morocco rose 25.1% (+23.7 MMDH) in 2025
Morocco's trade deficit with China reached 110.2 MMDH in 2025, up from 86.2 MMDH in 2024
Morocco's trade deficit with China was 21.7 MMDH in 2011
Imports from China rose by 23.8 MMDH in 2025

items.title: Maersk sets higher intermodal fuel fees for UK and Ireland landside moves in December
items.originalTitle: Maersk raises UK and Ireland intermodal fuel fees
items.summary: Maersk has announced revised Intermodal Fuel Fee levels for full-container-load landside transport in the United Kingdom and Ireland for December 2026. The UK fee is 11.6% for truck or rail transport, and Ireland's fee is 8.1% for truck transport.
items.impact: Forwarders and importers moving full containers inland in the UK and Ireland will pay a higher fuel surcharge on landside legs in December 2026. The UK rate applies to both truck and rail, so rail is not a cheaper alternative on this surcharge. Budgets for December inland haulage should be adjusted accordingly.
items.action: Check the December 2026 fuel fee table with Maersk and reflect the 11.6% UK and 8.1% Ireland levels in landside quotes. Watch for further monthly revisions.
keyFigures: UK intermodal fuel fee 11.6% for truck or rail in December 2026
Ireland intermodal fuel fee 8.1% for truck in December 2026

items.title: UK and EU agree food trade deal cutting SPS paperwork and border checks
items.originalTitle: Supermarket sweep: Morrisons, Tesco and M&S back Government's business-boosting food trade deal with Europe
items.summary: The UK and EU struck a food trade deal at the EU-UK Summit in Brussels, which the government says will remove costly paperwork and border checks for food and plants. Products such as fresh sausages, fresh burgers, seed potatoes and shellfish will regain access to the EU market, and food moving between Great Britain and Northern Ireland will also see reduced bureaucracy. The government estimates the deal could add up to £5.1bn to the UK economy in the long term.
items.impact: Forwarders and importers moving food and plants between the UK and EU should expect fewer certificates, less documentation and fewer border checks once the deal takes effect, which could cut costs per consignment and speed up transit. The article gives no start date, and retailers say the detail is still to be worked through, including regulatory alignment. Until then, existing SPS requirements still apply.
items.action: Monitor for the implementation date and the detailed SPS text, and identify which of your food and plant lines would benefit. Do not change certification or border procedures until the rules are confirmed in force.
keyFigures: Up to £5.1bn added to the UK economy in the long term
The EU took 58% of UK agri-food exports and supplied 69% of imports in 2025
Major agricultural exports to the EU could rise by around 16%
Food and drink exports to the EU have fallen by around a quarter in real terms since 2018

items.title: HMRC publishes guidance on added value duty calculation for mixed temporary export goods
items.originalTitle: Added value duty calculation where different temporary export goods are involved
items.summary: HMRC has published information on how added value duty is calculated where different temporary export goods are involved. The publisher's summary is brief and gives no further detail on the rules or figures.
items.impact: Importers and forwarders handling temporary exports from the UK that combine different goods may need to check how added value duty is worked out for their shipments. The short summary does not say what changes, so the exact effect on duty amounts or paperwork cannot be confirmed from this item alone.
items.action: Read the full HMRC guidance before the next temporary export shipment involving mixed goods, and check your duty calculations with your customs agent.

items.title: Hapag-Lloyd to replace fuel recovery surcharge with new Marine Fuel Surcharge from 2027
items.originalTitle: Hapag-Lloyd to introduce new Marine Fuel Surcharge for contracts from January 2027
items.summary: Hapag-Lloyd will introduce a new Marine Fuel Surcharge (MFS) for all contracts taking effect from 1 January 2027, gradually replacing its Marine Fuel Recovery (MFR) mechanism. The MFS reflects larger, more fuel-efficient vessels, changed operating speeds and a modelled full return to Suez Canal routings. Contracts taking effect before that date stay under the MFR until their terms end.
items.impact: Forwarders and importers should expect a different fuel surcharge structure on new contracts from 2027, with fuel costs reflected in freight rates through a revised mechanism. Only one fuel recovery mechanism applies to each contract at a time, so contract start dates will determine which surcharge applies. Quarterly adjustments continue under both mechanisms during the transition.
items.action: Check the start dates of upcoming contracts and quotes against the 1 January 2027 cut-off, and review how fuel surcharges are costed in 2027 pricing. Watch for the Q1 2027 MFS values published on Hapag-Lloyd's tariff page on 1 December 2026.
keyFigures: MFS applies to contracts taking effect on or after 1 January 2027
Q1 2027 MFS values to be published on 1 December 2026
MFS and MFR reviewed and adjusted quarterly
Existing contracts remain under MFR until the end of their agreed terms

items.title: IMO Net-Zero Framework faces compromise talks at December MEPC meeting
items.originalTitle: The Week in Alt Fuels: The net-zero bargain
items.summary: The IMO's Marine Environment Protection Committee meets from 30 November to 3 December to consider proposals ranging from stronger economic measures to removing greenhouse gas pricing altogether. The EU and Pacific Island states back the text approved in April 2025, while the US and several other countries, including major oil producers, want substantial changes to its technical and economic provisions. Shipping associations and some EU member states are pressing for a more flexible, achievable framework that avoids overlapping regional and global charges.
items.impact: A softer Net-Zero Framework could lower future carbon-related costs on ocean freight but could also make compliance cheaper than switching fuels, which may slow investment in cleaner fuels. Forwarders and importers should expect uncertainty over carbon pricing and surcharges until the outcome is clear. Any global deal that replaces overlapping regional charges, such as the EU's own measures, could change how carbon costs are levied on shipments.
items.action: Monitor the outcome of the IMO intersessional GHG working group (23 to 27 November) and the MEPC session (30 November to 3 December). Review contract clauses on bunker and carbon-related surcharges so you can adjust quickly once the framework is settled.
keyFigures: MEPC meets 30 November to 3 December
Intersessional GHG working group meets 23 to 27 November
Greece and three other EU states represent 70% of the EU-controlled fleet
Japan's proposal was not circulated within the six-month MARPOL period required for adoption at MEPC 85

items.title: Tentative deal averts strike threat at Los Angeles-Long Beach ports
items.originalTitle: Tentative union deal averts strike at Port of LA-Long Beach
items.summary: The Pacific Maritime Association and ILWU Local 26 have reached a tentative contract agreement covering about 250 watchmen at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, under federal mediation. The agreement is subject to ratification by Local 26 members, and the existing contract will be extended while that process runs. No terms or ratification timeline have been disclosed.
items.impact: The deal lowers the immediate risk of a labour disruption at the largest US container port complex, where a walkout could have affected cargo owners across the supply chain. Watchmen control terminal-gate access at six container terminals, so there were concerns that other union workers might honour their picket lines. Until ratification is confirmed, the risk is reduced rather than removed.
items.action: Keep monitoring for Local 26 ratification results and any published terms, and avoid treating the risk as closed until members vote. Check with carriers and terminals on any changes to gate or cargo handling arrangements at Los Angeles and Long Beach.
keyFigures: About 250 watchmen covered across six container terminals
Pre-settlement offer included a $3,200 one-time bonus
Offer would lift full-time watchman average earnings from over $170,000 to $198,000 a year
Local 26 represents roughly 2% of ILWU workers at the two ports

items.title: US trade groups urge deal as LA-Long Beach port security strike deadline nears
items.originalTitle: More Than 110 Trade Groups Urge Deal as LA-Long Beach Port Strike Deadline Nears
items.summary: More than 110 US trade associations urged the Pacific Maritime Association and ILWU Local 26 to reach a labour agreement before a contract extension expires at 12:01 a.m. Pacific time on Saturday. The dispute covers about 250 port security workers, and PMA said talks on 17 November made little progress. A related item in the source reports a tentative agreement between the PMA and the union for security workers.
items.impact: A strike could disrupt container operations at terminals handling much of Southern California's cargo, and thousands of longshore workers, clerks and foremen could honour picket lines. The associations warned that backlogs could take weeks or months to clear, with knock-on delays for trucking, rail and warehousing. Ports already face congestion from near-record import volumes.
items.action: Monitor the outcome of the tentative agreement and any ratification before Saturday's deadline, and review contingency plans for diverted or delayed Los Angeles and Long Beach bookings.
keyFigures: About 250 port security workers covered by the dispute
Local 26 represents about 2% of the ILWU workforce at the two ports
Six container terminals account for about 85% of cargo at Long Beach and 33% at Los Angeles
More than 110 trade associations signed the joint statement

items.title: Los Angeles and Long Beach labour group signs tentative truce with employers
items.originalTitle: LA-LB labour group signs truce with employers
items.summary: A labour group at the Los Angeles and Long Beach ports has reached a tentative agreement with employers, averting a strike. The deal is subject to ratification by rank-and-file port workers. The summary gives no further terms.
items.impact: A ratified deal would remove the immediate risk of strike-related disruption at two of the largest US container gateways. Until ratification is confirmed, forwarders should treat the risk of stoppage as not fully resolved. Contract terms, dates and any effect on cargo flows are not stated in the summary.
items.action: Monitor for the ratification vote result and watch for any strike notice at Los Angeles and Long Beach before finalising US import schedules.

items.title: Hapag-Lloyd to add equipment imbalance surcharge on intra-Asia Vietnam shipments
items.originalTitle: Hapag-Lloyd introduces Vietnam equipment surcharge
items.summary: Hapag-Lloyd will introduce an Equipment Imbalance Surcharge on intra-Asia shipments to Vietnam for dry and refrigerated containers loaded on sailings from 1 December 2026. The surcharge will stay in effect until further notice. The source summary lists per-container amounts for 20-foot dry, 40-foot dry and 40-foot high cube boxes, with the rest of the table not included.
items.impact: Forwarders and shipping agents moving containers into Vietnam on intra-Asia services will face an extra per-box charge from December 2026, adding to freight costs. The surcharge is linked to container imbalance, so it may be applied to cargo that already has a booking, depending on the carrier's terms. Costs should be built into quotes for Vietnam-bound boxes.
items.action: Check the full Hapag-Lloyd notice for the complete rate table, refrigerated container rates and any exemptions, and include the surcharge in forward quotes for Vietnam loadings from 1 December 2026.
keyFigures: 20-foot dry container: US$50 per container
40-foot dry container: US$100 per container
40-foot high cube container: US$100 per container

items.title: Spain bans scrubber wastewater discharge in all its ports from July 2027
items.originalTitle: Spain to ban all scrubber wastewater discharge in its ports
items.summary: Spain's Council of Ministers approved a royal decree banning ships fitted with any type of scrubber, whatever their flag, from discharging scrubber wastewater in its ports and anchorages from 1 July 2027. The ban covers open-loop, closed-loop and hybrid systems and replaces local restrictions at several Spanish ports, including Algeciras, Valencia and Barcelona. It aligns with the OSPAR Commission decision but goes further by bringing forward the closed-loop and hybrid ban and extending it beyond OSPAR areas.
items.impact: Ships with scrubbers will not be able to discharge washwater in Spanish ports and anchorages, so they must burn low-sulphur fuel in the regulated areas or hold wastewater on board for handover in port. This may add fuel costs and port-side handling for vessels calling Algeciras, Valencia, Barcelona and other Spanish ports. The uniform national rule should give operators more legal certainty than the current patchwork of local restrictions.
items.action: Vessel operators and agents calling Spanish ports should check which scrubber mode their ships use and plan low-sulphur fuel or wastewater handover arrangements before 1 July 2027. Monitor the royal decree text for detailed compliance requirements.
keyFigures: 7,230 ships currently equipped with scrubbers worldwide
Expected to rise to 7,612 vessels by 2029 (DNV)
Open-loop ban in OSPAR areas due by 1 July 2027, all scrubber modes by 1 July 2029
Denmark, Sweden and Finland banned open-loop discharges from 1 July 2025

items.title: JSV Group buys third ship for Alicante–Canary Islands express service
items.originalTitle: JSV puts third owned ship on Alicante–Canary Islands express service
items.summary: JSV Group has bought the 809 TEU containership CanariasGreen, previously chartered as Njord, for its express service from Alicante to the Canary Islands. The purchase, announced on 18 June 2026, gives the group three owned ships and greater control over its Canary Islands and Turkey connections.
items.impact: Owning rather than chartering a vessel gives JSV more control over capacity on the Alicante to Canary Islands link, which may support more consistent sailing schedules for cargo moving between mainland Spain and the islands. The source summary gives no details on rates, sailing frequency or transit times, so the practical effect on service levels is not yet clear.
items.action: Forwarders and agents moving cargo between Alicante and the Canary Islands should watch for schedule and capacity announcements from JSV on this service.
keyFigures: 809 TEU containership CanariasGreen
Three owned ships in the JSV Group fleet
Purchase announced 18 June 2026

items.title: Thames Freeport completes private 5G network across London Gateway and Tilbury ports
items.originalTitle: Thames Freeport completes private 5G network across London Gateway and Tilbury ports
items.summary: Verizon Business has completed a five-site private 5G network at Thames Freeport, covering London Gateway and the Port of Tilbury. The platform is already supporting trials of AI damage detection and digital truck processing.
items.impact: Digital truck processing and AI damage detection could, if rolled out, speed gate operations and cargo inspection at these Thames ports. For now the network is at trial stage, so day-to-day procedures and transit times are unlikely to change yet.
items.action: No immediate action needed. Monitor whether the trials move to wider operational use at London Gateway and Tilbury, and check with terminals on any new digital processes.
keyFigures: Five-site private 5G network

items.title: Sentury's Tangier tyre plant shifts exports from United States to Turkey
items.originalTitle: L’usine tangéroise de Sentury Tire redirige vers la Turquie une partie de ses pneus auparavant destinés aux États-Unis
items.summary: Sentury Tire's Tangier plant has begun selling part of its output in Turkey, previously destined for the United States, according to a Noria Research study. The US share of Moroccan car tyre exports fell from 94% in 2025 to 74% in the first half of 2026, while Turkey took 17% of shipments. The shift is attributed to higher US tariffs, and the group is also building a seven-million-tyre plant in Turkey.
items.impact: Forwarders handling Moroccan tyre exports may see more cargo routed to Turkey rather than the US, changing lanes and shipping volumes from Tanger Med. The study also reports that most of the plant's output leaves Morocco under temporary admission, which suspends duties on imported Chinese rubber and carbon black, so customs paperwork and inputs matter for compliance.
items.action: Check whether your Moroccan tyre volumes or lanes are affected by the shift from US to Turkish destinations, and review temporary admission documentation for Chinese inputs. No immediate action is needed beyond monitoring.
keyFigures: Moroccan car tyre exports reached about 1 billion dirhams in H1 2026, versus about 800 million in all of 2025
US share fell from 94% in 2025 to 74% in H1 2026; Turkey took 17% of shipments
Temporary admission covered 99.8% of Sentury's 2025 output leaving Morocco
Turkish plant: $272.8 million investment, 7 million tyres a year, 18-month build

items.title: Brazil's Mato Grosso plans for up to 3.8 million tonnes more fertiliser demand, citing OCP Morocco
items.originalTitle: Le Mato Grosso prévoit jusqu’à 3,8 millions de tonnes supplémentaires d’engrais et cite le Maroc dans sa stratégie logistique
items.summary: The Mato Grosso state economy secretariat published a Federal University of Mato Grosso study forecasting fertiliser demand rising 29% to 39% by 2034, adding 2.8 to 3.8 million tonnes on the 9.8 million tonnes used in 2024. The state already depends heavily on imports, with China, Canada and Russia supplying 69.6% of its 2025 fertiliser. Officials have held technical contacts with Moroccan producer OCP, under a federal memorandum with OCP Nutricrops that sets an indicative 3.8 million tonnes of phosphate fertiliser for Brazilian buyers in 2026-2027.
items.impact: For forwarders and importers, this points to a possible new long-haul bulk flow of Moroccan phosphate fertiliser to Brazil, from ports such as Jorf Lasfar. Each purchase remains subject to commercial terms still to be negotiated between OCP and buyers, so volumes and routings are not yet firm. Nothing in the text sets new costs, paperwork or transit times.
items.action: No action needed now. Monitor OCP export announcements and any Brazil-bound fertiliser capacity or booking offers for 2026-2027.

Mato Grosso received 11.4 million tonnes of fertiliser in 2025, 23.2% of Brazilian deliveries

OCP Jorf Lasfar declared capacity of 15 million tonnes a year

items.title: EU and Indonesia sign comprehensive trade and investment partnership agreements
items.originalTitle: EU and Indonesia sign ambitious trade and investment agreements
items.summary: The European Union and Indonesia have signed their Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) and Investment Protection Agreement (IPA). The source is a short publisher's summary, so details of tariff cuts, timelines and entry into force are not available here.
items.impact: The signing sets out a framework for future trade and investment rules between the EU and Indonesia, but it does not in itself change duties or procedures for cargo. Forwarders and importers should not assume new preferential rates until the agreements enter into force and the schedules are published.
items.action: Monitor the EU Official Journal and the Commission's trade pages for ratification steps, entry-into-force dates and tariff schedules for Indonesian goods.

items.title: EU and Indonesia sign CEPA trade deal opening market of 280 million consumers
items.originalTitle: EU and Indonesia sign CEPA opening a market of 280 million consumers
items.summary: The EU and Indonesia signed their Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement in Brussels on 21 November 2026, opening a market of 280 million consumers to EU exporters. The source summary indicates most Indonesian import duties are due to be phased out, with customs provisions also referenced, though the full text is truncated.
items.impact: Lower Indonesian import duties should make European goods cheaper to sell into Indonesia, which may lift export volumes through EU ports over time. Forwarders and agents should expect changes to customs documentation and origin requirements once the agreement is implemented, though the summary gives no detail on these. The timing of duty phase-outs is not stated in the material available.
items.action: Monitor the entry-into-force date and the tariff phase-out schedule for Indonesia, and review the full agreement text for origin and customs procedure changes before advising exporters.
keyFigures: Market of 280 million consumers
Signed 21 November 2026 in Brussels

items.title: EU bans plastic waste exports to Morocco and other non-OECD countries until May 2029
items.originalTitle: L’Union européenne interdit l’exportation de déchets plastiques vers le Maroc jusqu’en mai 2029 au minimum
items.summary: From 21 November, the EU prohibits exports of clean, non-hazardous plastic waste destined for recycling (basel code B3011) to non-OECD countries, including Morocco, for at least thirty months until 21 May 2029. The ban applies under EU Regulation 2024/1157 regardless of recycler capacity or the material's market value. Morocco had requested continued imports of European plastic waste, but the Commission removed plastics from its review of the Moroccan file.
items.impact: Recyclers in Morocco can no longer receive clean plastic waste shipments from EU companies, which removes a supply that totalled about 3,342 tonnes from EU origins in 2024. Forwarders must classify consignments carefully, since the line between waste for recycling and a secondary raw material is now a customs and environmental compliance question decided by authorities. Imports of polymers and recycled granules outside the waste category are not affected.
items.action: Review any consignments of plastic scrap or recyclable plastics from the EU to Morocco and confirm their waste classification with customs before shipping. Watch for the EU's May 2027 extension to other non-hazardous waste and the first list of admissible countries due before year end.
keyFigures: Ban runs until 21 May 2029, at least thirty months
EU exported about 1.4 million tonnes of plastic waste in 2025, roughly half to non-OECD countries
Morocco imported 7,567 tonnes of plastic waste in 2024, 3,342 tonnes of it from EU members
Turkey absorbed 510,000 tonnes of EU plastic waste in 2025

items.title: IMO decides on Net-Zero Framework and global shipping carbon pricing in December
items.originalTitle: Decision time on carbon pricing for global shipping at the UN
items.summary: Governments meet at the IMO from 23 November to 4 December 2026 to decide whether to adopt the Net-Zero Framework, which would introduce the world's first global carbon pricing for an industry. The framework combines progressively stricter carbon intensity targets with carbon pricing, and adoption was delayed in October 2025 by a close vote of 57 in favour and 49 against. Industry and NGO voices are split over whether any compromise will weaken fuel standards or allow fossil LNG and crop biofuels to count as transitional fuels.
items.impact: If adopted, the framework would add a carbon price to global shipping, which would feed into freight costs and surcharges on international routes. Delay or a weakened text could lead to regional and national rules, such as those already emerging in Africa and Europe, creating a regulatory patchwork for shippers and carriers. Investment decisions on fuels and fleet electrification are likely to hinge on the outcome.
items.action: Monitor the outcome of the ISWG-GHG-23 talks and MEPC 85 closely, and review exposure to carbon-linked surcharges on your main trade lanes before the decision on 4 December.
keyFigures: Global shipping represents about 5% of global oil demand
Adoption vote delayed in October 2025: 57 in favour, 49 against
Over 110 maritime companies and industry associations urged adoption this year
Over 30 maritime organisations committed to electricity reaching at least 20% of shipping energy use by 2035

items.title: Moroccan exports to China can enter duty-free under new Chinese scheme for African countries
items.originalTitle: Commerce extérieur : Les exportations marocaines vers la Chine exemptes de droits de douane
items.summary: Morocco's Ministry of Industry, Trade, Investment and Inclusive Economy has told exporters that goods shipped to the People's Republic of China may benefit from a 0% customs duty rate under a new Chinese trade measure for African countries. The ministry's circular urges exporters to study the rules of origin, which are attached, to confirm eligibility for preferential treatment.
items.impact: Eligible Moroccan products entering China should face no import duty, which could improve price competitiveness and open new export volumes. Exporters must meet the notified rules of origin to qualify, so product classification and supply chains need checking before shipments are booked. Certificates of origin for export are issued by the Administration des Douanes et Impôts Indirects, so paperwork must follow the current procedures.
items.action: Exporters should download the rules of origin attached to the circular, check product eligibility against them, and arrange certificates of origin with Moroccan Customs (ADII) before shipping to China.
keyFigures: 0% customs duty rate for eligible products exported to China

items.title: Morocco's 2027 budget bill cuts feed duties and exempts livestock and meat imports
items.originalTitle: PLF 2027: droits de douane réduits sur les aliments pour animaux et exonération sur les viandes
items.summary: Morocco's draft 2027 Finance Bill, as amended by the Chamber of Representatives, would cut import duties on animal feed raw materials from 40%, 30% and 10% to 2.5%. It would also exempt live bovine, ovine, caprine and camelid animals, and their fresh, chilled or frozen meat and offal, from import duties, subject to administrative procedures. The bill also introduces a 3% tax advance on duties for importers of goods for resale, reported by L'Economiste.
items.impact: Feed manufacturers should see lower input costs, which may ease livestock producers' costs over time. Importers of live animals and meat will face lower duty costs but must follow procedures set by the administration. Commercial importers of goods for resale will pay a 3% tax advance on customs duty value for 36 months from their first import, unless they hold a recent tax compliance certificate afterwards.
items.action: Monitor the final adopted text of the PLF 2027 for the actual rates, procedures and start dates, as the figures here are from a draft. Commercial importers should check their tax compliance status and prepare for the 3% advance payment.
keyFigures: Feed input duties cut from 40%, 30% and 10% to 2.5%
Tax advance of 3% of customs value for the first 36 months after first import
Tax compliance certificate valid for 30 days to avoid the advance after 36 months
Live animal and meat imports exempted from import duties

items.title: HMRC updates customs declaration document codes for UK and Northern Ireland imports and exports
items.originalTitle: Guidance: Data Element 2/3: Documents and Other Reference Codes (Union) of the Customs Declaration Service (CDS)
items.summary: HMRC has published a large update to Appendix 5A of the Customs Declaration Service guidance, which lists the document codes, status codes and details (such as licences and certificates) to declare in Data Element 2/3. Changes add, remove and amend many codes, including new codes for steel melt and pour requirements in Northern Ireland, EU Deforestation Regulation preparation, Russia and Belarus sanctions, and UK-India Free Trade Agreement preference claims.
items.impact: Declarants must use the correct document code, status code and document ID or reason for each licence, certificate or exemption, or declarations may be rejected or delayed. Several codes now require a document ID rather than a reason, and some status codes such as XW and XB have been withdrawn for certain codes. Northern Ireland declarations face new EU-aligned validation and requirements for steel, deforestation-related goods and sanctions, so paperwork and checks will increase for affected cargo.
items.action: Review the Appendix 5A entries for your commodity codes and update your declaration software and templates now, especially for Northern Ireland steel and deforestation-related goods. Check the Online Tariff for the conditions attached to each commodity code, since HMRC asks users to rely on those for associated document codes.
keyFigures: 1 October 2026: steel melt and pour requirements apply in Northern Ireland
30 December 2026: EU Deforestation Regulation introduced in Northern Ireland
15 July 2026: document code N954 used under the UK-India Free Trade Agreement
Document code C715 requires the FR5 prefix with the IOSS VAT number

items.title: UK proposes higher anti-dumping duties on Chinese tracked excavators after absorption review
items.originalTitle: TRA proposes increasing anti-dumping measure on excavators
items.summary: The Trade Remedies Authority has published initial findings in an absorption review of the anti-dumping measure on tracked excavators from China, finding that exporters have absorbed the duty so it is not protecting UK producers. It proposes increasing the duties for all exporters except Caterpillar Group, whose duty would be maintained at its current level because it has no current exports to the UK from China.
items.impact: Importers of tracked excavators from China, covering 360-degree revolving models between 11 and 80 tonnes, would face substantially higher anti-dumping duties if the proposal is adopted. Costs on affected machinery imports would rise, and forwarders and importers should expect shipments to be re-costed and entries to carry the new duty rates. Caterpillar Group goods would be unaffected by the change.
items.action: Importers and agents handling Chinese excavators should review their supplier duty rates now and consider submitting comments on the TRA public file before 7 December 2026 if affected.
keyFigures: Proposed anti-dumping duties of 40.18% to 80.16%
Measure imposed May 2025
Excavators of 11,000 kg to under 80,000 kg operating weight
Comments due before 7 December 2026

items.title: Morocco weighs 30% duty on polyester fibre, alarming bedding and textile manufacturers
items.originalTitle: Fibre de polyester : une hausse douanière qui inquiète les industriels de la literie
items.summary: A possible 30% customs duty on polyester staple fibre, used to fill mattresses, duvets and cushions, is worrying Moroccan textile and bedding manufacturers, who import most of this fibre. The article is truncated, so it does not confirm whether the duty has been adopted or when it would apply. Manufacturers fear higher prices would push consumers towards imported finished goods, hurting the sector and its jobs.
items.impact: If adopted, the duty would raise the landed cost of imported polyester fibre for Moroccan bedding and textile producers, which could feed through to higher prices for mattresses, duvets and cushions. Forwarders and importers handling fibre or related textile inputs may see changes in declared values and duty calculations. The article suggests the measure is still a scenario rather than a settled rule.
items.action: Monitor official announcements from Moroccan Customs (ADII) and the finance law for the final tariff decision, its scope and its effective date, and check whether any of your fibre or textile shipments fall under the affected tariff lines.
keyFigures: Proposed customs duty of 30% on polyester staple fibre
Industry fears higher consumer prices and job losses in the sector

items.title: EU keeps Tanger Med on transhipment lists for emissions trading and FuelEU Maritime
items.originalTitle: Tanger Med conserve sa qualification maritime européenne dans deux règlements sur les quotas d’émission et les carburants des porte-conteneurs
items.summary: The European Commission has kept Tanger Med on its list of non-EU transhipment ports, where a container ship call does not break the voyage calculation for EU climate obligations. Two implementing regulations, 2026/2562 and 2026/2563, also add the Egyptian ports of Abu Qir and Damietta, making four ports in total with East Port Said, and apply from 10 December.
items.impact: For container services transhipping at Tanger Med, the voyage is counted from the last legally recognised port, so emissions from the earlier leg stay in the EU calculation. The obligations fall on carriers rather than Moroccan terminals, but the cost of surrendering allowances under the EU ETS and of FuelEU Maritime compliance may feed into surcharges and routing decisions. Ships calling at intermediate ports with transhipment shares above 65% within 300 nautical miles of an EU port are now treated the same way.
items.action: Forwarders and agents using Tanger Med transhipment should ask carriers how the 10 December change affects their EU voyage calculations and any related surcharges. Monitor the list review, which must take place at least every two years.
keyFigures: Four listed ports: Abu Qir, Damietta, East Port Said and Tanger Med
Transhipment share above 65% of TEU and a distance below 300 nautical miles from an EU port
ETS surrender rate 70% for 2025 emissions and 100% for 2026 emissions
FuelEU Maritime reduction of 2% versus 2020, rising to 6% in 2030

items.title: IMO Net-Zero Framework stalls again as fund rules remain unwritten ahead of London talks
items.originalTitle: Analysis: IMO Net-Zero: now-or-never time draws near
items.summary: The IMO Net-Zero Framework was adjourned by a year in October 2025 after US threats, and the draft still does not say who holds the proposed fund or how its money is distributed. ISWG-GHG 23 opens in London on Monday, with the working group meeting 23 to 27 November and MEPC 85 following from 30 November. The article argues that the fund's proceeds, the reward method and a post-2030 price path must be settled before any vote.
items.impact: If adopted, the framework would add a global levy on top of the EU ETS and FuelEU, and carriers would have no vote over the fund. The US opposes it and has threatened visa penalties, port fees and sanctions, so adoption remains uncertain. Existing EU carbon costs continue regardless of the IMO outcome.
items.action: Watch the outcome of ISWG-GHG 23 and MEPC 85 for written fund rules, the reward method and the post-2030 price path. Check freight contracts for how ETS and FuelEU costs are passed through to shippers.
keyFigures: Adoption adjourned by a year in October 2025, by 57 votes to 49 with 21 abstentions
Remedial unit prices of $100 and $380 fixed only to 2030
Reward method due by 1 March 2027; post-2030 mechanism due by 1 January 2028
Shipping's annual EU ETS bill estimated at about €9bn at €100 a tonne

items.title: Mediterranean spot rates rise 6.8% as Red Sea container return stalls
items.originalTitle: Xeneta Weekly Ocean Container Shipping Market Update: Mediterranean spot rates move in mysterious ways as Red Sea return stalls
items.summary: Far East to Mediterranean spot rates rose 6.8% in the past week to USD 4,989 per FEU on 19 November 2026, while rates on other Far East fronthaul routes continued to soften. Xeneta links the divergence to a November slowdown in container ship transits through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which fell 28% from a peak of 16.6 per day on 25 October to 11.9 on 19 November.
items.impact: Mediterranean-bound cargo from the Far East now costs USD 1,551 per FEU more than North Europe-bound cargo, so budgets for Mediterranean lanes need adjusting. Far East to Mediterranean trades are the most exposed to Red Sea disruption, which can cause sudden rate spikes. Xeneta expects rates to trend downwards into 2027, but not smoothly.
items.action: Monitor Bab el-Mandeb transit counts and Mediterranean spot rates over the coming weeks, and build flexibility and rate contingency into bookings for Far East to Mediterranean cargo.
keyFigures: Far East to Mediterranean spot rate USD 4,989 per FEU, up 6.8% week on week
Mediterranean premium over North Europe USD 1,551 per FEU
Bab el-Mandeb container transits fell 28% from 16.6 per day peak to 11.9 on 19 November
Far East to North Europe spot rate USD 3,438 per FEU

items.title: Transpacific container spot rates fall while Asia-Med rates unexpectedly spike
items.originalTitle: Transpac spots finally on the slide, but Asia-Med spike a surprise
items.summary: Container spot rates on the transpacific fell for a seventh consecutive week, with Shanghai-New York down 9% to $8,194 per 40ft and Shanghai-Los Angeles down 5% to $7,026. Asia-Mediterranean rates rose instead: Shanghai-Genoa was up 6% to $4,436 per 40ft after three weeks of flat rates, while Shanghai-Rotterdam was unchanged at $3,496. European forwarders said the Asia-Med rise did not match demand or space conditions.
items.impact: Forwarders and importers may see transpacific costs ease in early December, although the US west coast forwarder Freight Right expects rates to stay largely stable and carriers to hold baseline pricing ahead of January. Asia-Med shippers face notified increases of new FAK levels and pre-Chinese New Year peak season surcharges of $1,000 to $1,600 per 40ft, but forwarders doubt these will fully stick. New capacity arriving on the transpacific over the next two to three weeks, including Zim's ZX3 and MSC's Mustang service, adds further downward pressure.
items.action: Watch whether the first-half December Asia-Med increases and the peak season surcharges hold, and look for vessel-specific transpacific promotional rates in early December before committing to bookings.
keyFigures: Shanghai-Genoa spot rate up 6% to $4,436 per 40ft
Shanghai-New York down 9% to $8,194 per 40ft
Pre-Chinese New Year peak season surcharges of $1,000-$1,600 per 40ft

items.title: Shippers criticise carriers' peak season surcharges and capacity limits amid weak oversight
items.originalTitle: Container shipping rate tactics draw competition criticism
items.summary: Shippers complain about a lack of regulatory oversight in container shipping, as carriers seek to raise earnings through peak season surcharges while restricting capacity. The publisher's summary gives no further detail on specific carriers, routes or amounts.
items.impact: Forwarders and importers may face higher peak season surcharges and tighter space availability on container services. Without clear regulatory oversight, shippers have limited recourse against surcharge levels.
items.action: Check surcharge schedules with carriers and forwarders before booking peak season cargo, and secure space early where possible. Monitor for any regulatory response on surcharges and capacity.

items.title: Drewry World Container Index falls 3% to $4,176 as Transpacific rates keep dropping
items.originalTitle: Drewry: World Container Index Down 3% Last Week
items.summary: The Drewry World Container Index fell 3% to $4,176 per 40ft container in the week to 19 November 2026, driven by lower Transpacific rates, though it remains 126% higher year on year. Shanghai to New York rates dropped 9% to $8,194 and Shanghai to Los Angeles fell 5% to $7,026, both continuing a seven-week downward trend. On Asia-Europe/Med, Shanghai to Genoa rose 6% to $4,436 while Shanghai to Rotterdam held at $3,496.
items.impact: Transpacific shippers should see continued rate softening as carriers cut capacity through blank sailings, with ten announced for next week. Asia-Europe costs are likely to rise in December as carriers push peak season surcharges of $1,000 to $1,600 per 40ft ahead of the new contract season. North Europe port congestion is delaying empty container returns to Asia, raising risk of equipment shortages.
items.action: Monitor Transpacific rates, which Drewry expects to fall further next week, and consider timing bookings accordingly. For Asia-Europe, budget for the proposed PSS surcharges effective December and watch for equipment availability given the North Europe congestion.
keyFigures: WCI composite $4,176 per 40ft, down 3% week on week, up 126% year on year
Shanghai to New York $8,194 per 40ft, down 9%, lowest in 15 weeks

items.title: EU and UK conclude talks to link their emissions trading systems
items.originalTitle: EU and UK agree to link Emission Trading Systems (ETS)
items.summary: The EU and UK have concluded negotiations to link their Emissions Trading Systems, announced at the EU-UK summit on 20 November. The linking agreement is committed to apply from 2028, subject to ratification and entry into force in both jurisdictions. It paves the way for a possible mutual exemption from each side's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism.
items.impact: Once the linking agreement is in force, UK-origin goods would be exempt from the EU CBAM after the EU amends Annex III through a delegated act, and a corresponding UK approach is expected. This would remove double carbon charges and reduce paperwork and costs for businesses trading across the Channel. The exemption is not yet in place and depends on ratification and legal steps in both jurisdictions.
items.action: Monitor ratification progress and the Commission's delegated act amending Annex III, and keep current CBAM declaration processes for UK-origin goods until any exemption takes effect.
keyFigures: Linking agreement committed to apply as of 2028
Summit announcement made on 20 November 2026

items.title: UK-EU carbon market link to extend UK ETS to international shipping from 2028
items.originalTitle: UK-EU carbon market link brings international shipping into UK ETS
items.summary: The linkage of the UK and EU carbon markets will extend the UK Emissions Trading Scheme to international shipping from 2028. The publisher's summary also notes a separate FuelEU-style regime that may create further obligations, though the article text is truncated.
items.impact: Shipping lines and agents calling at UK ports would face carbon costs on international voyages from 2028, which may feed into surcharges and freight pricing. A parallel FuelEU-style regime could add separate fuel-intensity compliance requirements. Forwarders should expect cost pass-through once the rules take effect.
items.action: Monitor the detailed UK-EU linkage text and carrier surcharge announcements, and ask carriers how they plan to handle UK ETS and FuelEU-style costs on 2028 sailings.

items.title: UK Chamber of Shipping urges UK-EU reset to cut ETS and trade costs
items.originalTitle: UK-EU reset must reduce costs for trade and shipping
items.summary: The UK Chamber of Shipping is asking the UK and EU to use reset talks on 20 November to reduce trade barriers, cut regulatory costs and support shipping's net zero transition. It urges closer alignment on ETS monitoring, reporting and verification, and wants ETS revenues returned to shipping's decarbonisation. It also calls for protection of ferry, short-sea and lifeline services and progress towards a UK-EU SPS agreement.
items.impact: These are recommendations from industry rather than adopted rules, so no immediate change to costs, paperwork or transit times is confirmed. If the UK extends its ETS internationally or the two sides align emissions monitoring, costs could flow through to UK imports, exports and consumers. Ferry and short-sea operators could also face changes to derogations and border controls.
items.action: No action is needed yet. Monitor the outcome of the reset talks, any UK ETS expansion proposals and changes to SPS or border control arrangements affecting Northern Ireland and ferry routes.
keyFigures: UK-EU reset talks held on 20 November
Chamber calls for an economic impact assessment before any international UK ETS extension

items.title: Moroccan port traffic rises 3.1% to 202.7 million tonnes by end September
items.originalTitle: Maroc: le trafic portuaire augmente de 3,1% à fin septembre 2026
items.summary: Morocco's ports handled 202.7 million tonnes of commercial traffic to the end of September, up 3.1% on the same period last year, according to the Ministry of Equipment and Water. Transhipment grew 7.4% to 105.2 million tonnes and now accounts for 51.9% of total traffic, while domestic traffic fell 1.3% and exports fell 2.4%. Container volumes rose 2.5% to 9.6 million TEU, and phosphate traffic dropped 15.7%.
items.impact: Growth is driven by transhipment, so Moroccan ports are increasingly serving vessels passing through the Strait of Gibraltar rather than cargo for the domestic market. Forwarders may see continued strength in container capacity, but exporters and phosphate shippers face weaker volumes. Cabotage and bunkering declines suggest reduced domestic coastal and fuel activity.
items.action: Monitor berth congestion and container availability at Tanger Med and other Moroccan hubs as transhipment volumes keep rising, and check phosphate and cereal shipment plans against the reported declines.
keyFigures: Total traffic 202.7 million tonnes, up 3.1%
Transhipment 105.2 million tonnes, up 7.4%
Containers 9.6 million TEU, up 2.5%
Phosphates 21.7 million tonnes, down 15.7%

items.title: EU Customs Authority holds first management board meeting in Lille, elects chairperson
items.originalTitle: EU Customs Authority holds first management board meeting in Lille
items.summary: The European Union Customs Authority (EUCA) held its first management board meeting in Lille, electing Malgorzata Krok of Poland as Chairperson and adopting core governance and administrative procedures. The agency is a key part of the EU Customs Reform, which entered into force in September, and will coordinate national customs administrations and support EU-level risk analysis. Its activities are scheduled to begin as soon as possible in 2027, with full capacity foreseen after 2030.
items.impact: For forwarders and importers, the EUCA will gradually shift customs risk analysis and controls towards common EU priorities, and it will develop the EU Customs Data Hub to replace over 100 national customs systems. Near-term effects on declarations and clearance are unlikely, as the agency only begins operating in 2027 and reaches full capacity after 2030. Longer term, expect more harmonised controls across Member States.
items.action: No immediate action is required. Monitor EUCA setup milestones and EU Customs Data Hub timelines, and plan for changes to national systems as they migrate.
keyFigures: Around 300 staff at full capacity
Data Hub will replace over 100 national systems
Activities to begin as soon as possible in 2027
Full capacity foreseen after 2030

items.title: IMO's MEPC 85 faces divide over Net-Zero Framework adoption
items.originalTitle: MEPC 85 to confront net-zero divide
items.summary: The IMO's Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85) meets in London to resolve differences over draft MARPOL Annex VI amendments and mid-term greenhouse gas measures under the 2023 IMO strategy. The Clean Shipping Coalition urges adoption of the Net-Zero Framework 'as is' before the end of the year, while the Union of Greek Shipowners criticises the EU's negotiating stance and calls for a broader, more flexible approach.
items.impact: The outcome could set a global fuel standard and economic mechanism for international shipping, affecting future fuel and operating costs. Continued delay keeps uncertainty over the sector's decarbonisation pathway, making long-term cost planning harder for forwarders, agents and importers.
items.action: No immediate action is required; monitor the MEPC 85 outcome and any decision on adopting the Net-Zero Framework before year end.
keyFigures: Net-Zero Framework first approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025
Adoption blocked in October 2025, with the adjournment set for one year

items.title: Höegh Autoliners says China's green fuel dominance grows as IMO paralysis persists
items.originalTitle: IMO paralysis is accelerating China’s green fuel dominance, warns Höegh Autoliners
items.summary: Höegh Autoliners chief executive Andreas Enger says China's rapidly improving green fuel economics are increasingly shaping investment decisions. The publisher's summary is cut off, but the headline links this trend to IMO paralysis on decarbonisation rules.
items.impact: The summary gives no detail on specific rules, prices or dates. The direction is that investment in green fuels for shipping may increasingly follow Chinese economics while global IMO action stalls, which could shape future fuel supply and vessel investment choices.
items.action: No immediate action needed. Monitor IMO decisions on shipping emissions and Chinese green fuel supply developments, and read the full article for detail.
